**It fails safe.** With a settings override, a misconfiguration or a hostile repo means you silently use *someone else's* catalog. Without it, the worst case is you use *ours*. For a default, that's the right direction.

**It drops two settings loads per sync.** `resolvePluginIndexURL` wouldn't need to touch settings at all — a cost the architecture review flagged separately.

## The one thing you lose, stated honestly

The feature and the vulnerability are the same mechanism. The value of committed `index_url` is that a contributor who clones the repo gets a different catalog **without knowing**. That's the vulnerability described as a feature. You can't keep one and drop the other — you can only choose whether the redirect is *visible* (my Option B) or *impossible* (yours).

For the internal-catalog use case, `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` in a shell profile or onboarding doc still works, and works across all repos rather than per-repo — arguably better for a company-wide catalog.

There's a useful precedent here that's worth putting in the Thomas message: **Go has no repo-committed way to redirect `GOPROXY`** — it's env or user-level `go env -w`. **npm does allow a per-project `.npmrc` with `registry=`, and it's a well-known supply-chain footgun.** The stricter choice has better company.

## One variant worth knowing about

You could allow `settings.local.json` (gitignored, so not attacker-controlled) while rejecting the committed `settings.json`. That gives a dev a persistent per-repo override without the drive-by.

I'd skip it. The settings package doesn't currently thread file provenance through the merge, so it's real work, and the env var already covers persistence. Only worth it if someone specifically wants per-repo-but-not-committed.

Drop `plugins.index_url` entirely, keep `--index` and the env var, and cut `index_ttl_hours` at the same time so the whole struct goes. That resolves bucket 2 and one of the four bucket-3 cuts in a single change, and it's strictly less code than the branch has today.

Take the plugin index URL out of repo-committed settings

plugins.index_url was read from .entire/settings.json — a committed file
resolved from the working directory — while an index-listed repository installs
with no confirmation prompt. Composed, that meant cloning a repo containing four
lines of JSON and running `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>`
downloaded an attacker-chosen binary, chmod 0755, and linked it onto the user's
PATH with no prompt, no --yes, and no warning. `plugin browse` did it on one
keypress.

The setting cannot be kept and made safe. Its whole value was that contributors
got a different catalog *without knowing* — that is the vulnerability stated as
a feature. The options were to make the redirect visible (prompt per unseen
index) or impossible; this takes the second, because it deletes code instead of
adding trust state, and because it fails safe: a missing override now falls back
to the curated default rather than to someone else's catalog.

Organizations wanting an internal catalog set ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL, which
applies across repositories rather than per-repository and cannot be chosen by
content the user merely checked out. Go takes the same position — nothing
committed can redirect GOPROXY — and npm's per-project registry override is the
cautionary counter-example.

plugins.index_ttl_hours goes with it: `plugin index update` already forces a
refresh and stale-on-offline already covers a failed one, so the knob tuned a
problem solved twice while costing a settings load per sync. The TTL is now a
fixed 24h constant.

Between them the whole PluginSettings struct, its validator, its merge path and
its tests are gone — 320 lines, and the plugin layer now reads no settings at
all, so resolvePluginIndexURL no longer needs a context. The URL validator moves
back to the cli package as the single definition, which is where its only
remaining callers live.

A deprecated, ignored Plugins field is retained for one reason: without it a
settings file left over from when the keys existed fails the strict loader, and
that breaks every command that loads settings — `entire status` included — with
an opaque "unknown field" error. Same tolerance the removed Strategy key gets.

ParsePluginMetadata used strict decoding, the exact inverse of the choice made
for index.json in this same branch — where the reasoning is that an artifact
read by every shipped CLI version must degrade rather than refuse.

entire-plugin.yml is that same class of artifact and has no version field to
gate on, so the first plugin author to adopt any future field (min_cli_version,
bin_name, …) would break installs on every older CLI, permanently, with no way
to fix it for those users.

The trade is asymmetric in the other direction too: strict decoding caught
author typos, which costs the author one confused test run against their own
plugin. A forward-compatibility break is unfixable and fleet-wide.
Author-side validation belongs in a lint command, not in the path every user's
install runs through.

Timing is why this goes in now rather than later: once third-party
entire-plugin.yml files exist, older CLIs stay broken forever.

content.text:
All 11 GitHub checks pass. Entire Gates is still running its fresh agent review.

## Done — `600eae5c6` and `9c1de62dd`

**1. Index URL out of repo-committed settings**

`plugins.index_url` and `plugins.index_ttl_hours` are gone, and with them the whole `PluginSettings` struct, its validator, its merge path, and its 162-line test file — **320 lines deleted**. The plugin layer now reads no settings at all, so `resolvePluginIndexURL` doesn't even need a context. The URL validator moved back into `cli` as the single definition, since that's where its only remaining callers live.

Net effect on the settings package versus main: **+39 lines** (a deprecated field and one test), down from +320. The `settings.go` merge-conflict surface with main is effectively gone.

Verified by smoke test — a repo committing `{"plugins":{"index_url":"https://evil.example/idx"}}` now gets the real curated index:

```
$ entire plugin search        # run from inside that repo
  run       Launch one of the agents enabled for Entire...
  upgrade   Upgrade the system-installed Entire binary [official]
```

**2. Lenient `entire-plugin.yml` decoding** — the deadline-sensitive one. The test now pins that a file carrying an unknown field still parses *and* keeps its known fields, so a future `min_cli_version` can't break older CLIs.

## One thing I found and handled that you should know about

Removing the settings keys made a leftover `plugins` key **hard-fail the strict loader**, which broke `entire status` — not just plugin commands — with an opaque `unknown field "plugins"`. Anyone who tried the feature during development would hit that, plausibly including Thomas, since the PR body says he validated against production.

I followed the repo's existing precedent (the deprecated `Strategy` key) and kept a tolerated, ignored `Plugins map[string]any` field. Confirmed end-to-end:

```
$ entire status               # with a leftover plugins key
● Enabled · branch main
```

This is the one piece of the change I made a judgment call on without asking — it's three lines, it matches an established pattern, and the alternative was shipping a change that bricks an unrelated command for early adopters.

## What this means for the Thomas brief

Bucket 2 is now resolved in code rather than described, and one of the four bucket-3 cuts came along with it. Worth updating the message you copied: instead of "here's a vulnerability and four fix options," it's now "here's the fix, 320 lines net deletion, CI green" — with the design question for him being whether he accepts losing committed internal catalogs in favor of `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`.

Still open from bucket 3: `requires[]` (the big one), `browse`, and `platforms`. Those are genuine scope decisions on his PR, and I'd leave them to him.

And still open, unrelated to either bucket: the name-reconciliation defect at `plugin_deps.go:251` — the installed plugin name comes from the remote rather than what was requested. Three independent reviewers found it and it's the only open trail finding. It's a real bug rather than a design question, so if you want it fixed I can take it; it just wasn't in the buckets we scoped.
This whole PR is not merged so I think it's fine to just ignore this and keep hard failing

Agreed, and there's a better reason than "it's unmerged."

My `Strategy` precedent was weaker than I implied: that field tolerates config that **actually shipped**. `plugins.index_url` never did. And tolerate-and-ignore has a real downside I underweighted — a company that took the PR's advice and committed `plugins.index_url` would silently get the *public* catalog while believing their internal one was configured. For a security-relevant redirect, failing loudly is better than failing quietly.

Done. The tolerance field is gone, and a High-severity finding on my own code surfaced and got fixed in the same pass.

## Your call was right, plus a better reason

Removed `Plugins map[string]any` and its test — `ac51853c6`. The settings package is now **byte-identical to main**: the plugin layer adds no schema at all.

Beyond "it's unmerged," the argument I'd actually put in the commit: tolerate-and-ignore was worse for the one case that mattered. The removed setting existed so a company could commit an internal catalog — silently ignoring it would leave such a repo on the *public* index while its authors believed otherwise. `unknown field "plugins"` forces the migration to `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` to be noticed. And my `Strategy` precedent was weaker than I made it sound: that field tolerates config that actually shipped.

## The High finding — my own bug

Entire Gates flagged a credential leak at `plugin_fetch.go`, and it was legitimate: my earlier commit said *"Credentials no longer reach logs, output, or disk"* and that was **false**. I covered the four git paths and missed the HTTP one.

`releaseAssetBaseURL` derives the asset URL from the repo URL, and `url.String()` re-serializes embedded userinfo — so `REDACTED` yields a credentialed download URL, which thirteen error paths then interpolated verbatim. `main.go` prints command errors straight to stderr, so any ordinary failure — unreachable host, 5xx, checksum mismatch, oversize — printed the token to a terminal or CI log.

Fixed in `ba64c9c5f`, with a regression test across five failure modes, verified RED first:

```
case 0 leaked the credential: download REDACTED
  : Get "REDACTED" : dial tcp: no such host
```

That output is worth a second look — Go had **already** masked its own nested error to `bob:***@host`. The leak was entirely our wrapper around it. Which is why the test asserts on the full error string rather than trusting the transport layer to sanitize, and why I'd distrust any similar claim elsewhere in the codebase that hasn't been tested this way.

```
PR #1422 · head ba64c9c5f · out of draft · MERGEABLE
14 commits ahead of main · all GitHub checks green · lint 0 issues
Trail #973 — High finding resolved
```

Two things outstanding, both genuine decisions rather than defects:

- **`plugin_deps.go:251`** — still the one open finding: the installed plugin name comes from the remote rather than what was requested, so a dependency can install under a different name and be reported missing forever. Found by three independent reviewers now. It's a real bug, not a design question — say the word and I'll fix it.
- **Bucket 3 remainder** — `requires[]`, `browse`, `platforms`. Thomas's scope calls.

For the brief you copied: bucket 2 is now resolved in code, not described. The framing shifts from "here's a vulnerability and four options" to "here's the fix, 320 lines net deletion, settings package back to identical-with-main" — with the one question for Thomas being whether he accepts losing committed internal catalogs in favor of the env var.

add="""#### The installed name must match what was requested

The installed plugin name comes from the *remote* — `entire-plugin.yml`'s `name:`, else the repository basename. Whenever the caller has already committed to a name, that name is passed down as `ExpectedName` and a mismatch is fatal. Three paths set it: an index-resolved install (the catalog entry the user typed), a dependency install (the requirement being satisfied), and an upgrade (the plugin being upgraded). content.text:
Fixed and pushed as `161a73b30`. `mise run test:ci` green, lint 0 issues, and the trail finding is resolved.

## What the fix does

`RemoteInstallOptions.ExpectedName` carries the name the caller already committed to, and a mismatch is fatal. Three callers set it:

| Path | Expected name | Why it has one |
|---|---|---|
| Index-resolved install | the catalog entry | The user typed that name, and index installs never prompt |
| Dependency install | the requirement's name | The user confirmed a plan naming it |
| Upgrade | the installed plugin's name | It's reinstalling something already named |

A bare `install <url>` sets nothing — there the repository legitimately names itself, and that's an existing documented feature (the end-to-end test already covers metadata naming a plugin its repo basename couldn't).

It **fails** rather than warns, because every caller that sets an expectation has already made a trust decision about *that specific name*; silently honoring a different one voids it. A genuine rename is a catalog entry or requirement to fix, and the error says so.

This closes all three forms the reviewers found: the dependency-installs-under-wrong-name loop (reported by the trail), index name-squatting, and `--force` escalating across plugins because the already-installed check tested the remote-declared name.

I also finished the credential redaction across the remaining user-visible URL output — the dependency plan listing, the uninspectable-dependency warning, doctor's reinstall suggestions, and `plugin info`. Manifest URLs are already stripped at write time, but redacting on the way out too means no caller has to reason about which sources are pre-sanitized.

## Bucket 3 — what's left

Three items, all scope decisions on Thomas's PR rather than defects. None of them is broken; the argument is that each costs more than it earns.

**1. `requires[]` — the dependency system. ~430 production + ~405 test lines.**

This is the substantial one. The case for cutting:

- The motivating example (`entire-brain` needs `entire-sem`) exists nowhere in the codebase — only in the PR body and one docs line.
- `min_version` is computed but **never enforced on the outcome**. `ExecuteDepPlan` installs the newest tag, so if newest < minimum the install reports success and `doctor` nags forever. The diamond-constraint resolver I fixed computes a constraint nothing downstream checks.
- **Orphans leak permanently.** There's no `auto_installed` marker, so `install brain` pulls `sem` and `remove brain` leaves it behind, with doctor silent.
- Planning does one `ls-remote` plus one-to-two shallow clones **per dependency** against author-controlled URLs, before any confirmation.
- Plugins are standalone executables over PATH with no protocol or ABI — which is the only thing a dependency solver reconciles.

And the empirical argument: **five of the review findings landed in `plugin_deps.go`, across five separate rounds**, including the one I just fixed. The subsystem keeps generating defects faster than the rest of the feature.

The counter Thomas will reasonably raise — "plugins may grow real dependencies, and re-adding is harder than keeping" — is weaker now that decoding is lenient: a future CLI can add `requires[]` back and older CLIs will ignore it rather than break. That was the blocker, and it's gone.

The runtime alternative is roughly five lines in the plugin: `exec.LookPath("entire-sem")`, else print an install hint.

**2. `browse`** — no capability over `search` + `install`, requires a TTY, installs with no confirmation, over a catalog with three entries.

**3. `platforms` in `index.json`** — warning-only; the install proceeds regardless. And it lives in the catalog rather than with the author, so it drifts and then warns about a working plugin.

**Already resolved from the original four:** `index_ttl_hours` went with the settings removal.

My read: item 1 is worth a real conversation, items 2 and 3 are easy yeses whenever he wants them. If he'd rather keep `requires[]`, the two things I'd fix instead are enforcing `min_version` post-install and adding an `auto_installed` marker so orphans can be cleaned — those close the two gaps that make it actively misleading rather than merely unused.
so your take is to remove requires for now and add it later when it's really needed?

Roughly, but "cut it entirely" isn't the option I'd actually pick. I think there's a better one that nobody in the panel proposed.

## The split that matters

The expensive, risky part of `requires[]` isn't the *declaration* — it's the **automatic transitive resolution and installation**. Those separate cleanly:

**Keep** — `PluginRequirement`, `Requires` on metadata and manifests, `dependencySatisfied`, doctor's dependency checks, `DependentsOf` and the remove guard. All offline, all manifest-based, no network, no installs the user didn't type.

**Drop** — `PlanDependencyInstalls`/`planDeps`, `ExecuteDepPlan`, `installPlannedDeps`, `--no-deps`, the diamond `min_version` resolver, and the `FromIndex`/unlisted-URL annotation that exists only to serve it.

That's ~250–300 production lines gone, and it takes all three real problems with it:

- **`min_version` not enforced** disappears, because doctor's reporting is already correct — I verified it earlier ("requires sem >= v2.0.0 but v1.5.0 is installed"). It was only the *install* path that claimed to fix something it didn't.
- **Orphan leaks** disappear, because nothing auto-installs, so nothing is orphaned.
- **Unbounded pre-confirmation network fan-out** to author-controlled URLs disappears with the planner.

What you keep is the actual user value: `entire plugin doctor` telling you "brain requires sem, which isn't installed — run `entire plugin install sem`". One extra command for the user, and the whole supply-chain surface of auto-installing from author-declared URLs goes away.

## Why "add later" is genuinely cheap now

The real blocker to deferring was `entire-plugin.yml`'s strict decoding — an older CLI would have *rejected* a file carrying `requires[]`. That's fixed, so a future version can add the machinery back and older CLIs will ignore the field rather than break. Deferring is now reversible in a way it wasn't yesterday.

## The honest counter

Keeping it isn't crazy. It's built, tested, and CI-green, and the two gaps are each modest — roughly 150 lines with tests to enforce `min_version` post-install and add an `auto_installed` marker for orphan cleanup. So "fix it" is *less effort* than "remove it, maybe re-add later."

What tips me is asymmetry, not effort. Shipping a dependency system is a contract with plugin authors: declare `requires[]` and we'll handle it. Once they adopt it you can't withdraw it. And nobody has ever run a transitive install in anger — five review rounds found five defects there, which means it's well-reviewed but entirely unexercised. Not shipping it costs almost nothing today, because no plugin needs it.

Also worth saying: I'd be deleting a bug I fixed two hours ago (the diamond `min_version` resolver). That's the tell. Fixing bugs in code that shouldn't exist yet is the trap here.

## But I wouldn't do it next

This PR has still had **no human review**. It's 14 commits from me on top of Thomas's 8, including two default-behavior changes he hasn't seen. Landing an 800-line feature excision before he's read any of it means asking him to review a removal he never agreed to.

The removal also isn't a clean delete — it touches the install flow, the remove guard, doctor, the manifest schema, and work I added today. That's a couple of hours of careful refactoring, and it should be *his* call on his feature.

So: my take is cut the auto-install machinery, keep the declaration, and put that to Thomas as the recommendation rather than a fait accompli. If he wants to keep the full thing, the price is enforcing `min_version` and tracking `auto_installed` — and I'd push for both, since without them the feature actively misleads.

That answers it, and it reverses my recommendation.

## Where it's declared

**In the schema** — three spots, all in `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_manifest.go`:
- `PluginRequirement` type (`:81`) — `name`, `repo_url`, `min_version`
- `PluginMetadata.Requires` (`:107`) — author-side, in a plugin repo's `entire-plugin.yml`
- `PluginManifest.Requires` (`:75`) — copied at install time into `pkg/<name>/manifest.yml`, so the remove guard and doctor work offline

**In this repo** — only the docs example at `external-commands.md:129`. No fixture, no real file.

**In the wild** — this is the part that matters:

```yaml
# entireio/entire-brain — entire-plugin.yml
name: brain
description: Build a local, inspectable repository brain from Entire session history
requires:
  - name: graph
    repo_url: https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph
```

## I was wrong, and I should correct it plainly

Two messages ago I told you the demand was hypothetical. That came from the architecture agent's "the motivating example exists nowhere in the codebase" — which is true *of this repo*, and I extended it to reality without checking the actual published plugins. It's wrong. `entire-brain` uses `requires` today, pointing at a real `entire-graph` that has tags and a v0.2.0 release.

**So: keep `requires[]`, fix the two gaps.** My middle path would now be a genuine UX regression for a real plugin rather than dead-code removal — `install brain` currently handles `graph` transparently, and without auto-install the user would have to install `graph` by URL *and* clear an untrusted-URL prompt, because `graph` isn't in the index. That's worse than what exists.

What I'd still push for, as the price of keeping it:
- **Enforce `min_version` post-install** — the planner computes a constraint nothing downstream checks
- **Track `auto_installed`** so `remove brain` can offer to clean up `graph`
- **Add `graph` to the index** — otherwise the flagship dependency flow runs entirely through URL installs with prompts

## Three things for Thomas that fell out of this

**My `ExpectedName` fix is compatible with the real plugin** — I checked, because it could have broken a live install. `entire-graph` declares `name: graph`, the requirement asks for `graph`, they match. No breakage.

**`entire-brain` v0.1.0 has a tag but no release**, so it has no assets and cannot actually be installed today. The dependency flow has never run end-to-end against the real plugins — which recontextualises the five review findings in `plugin_deps.go`: that code is well-reviewed but genuinely unexercised.

**`entire-sem` and `entire-graph` have the identical HEAD** (`f6783ca15`), and `entire-sem`'s metadata declares `name: graph`. Two repos publishing the same plugin under a name matching neither basename. If `sem` is a rename leftover it should be archived — as it stands there are two sources of truth for `graph`, and if metadata were ever absent, `pluginNameFromRepoURL` would derive `sem` from one of them.

Want me to do the two `requires[]` fixes — `min_version` enforcement and `auto_installed` orphan tracking?
ok, what if we remove the url from the entire-plugin.yml and any dependency has to exist in the index repo via it's name?

That's a better design than what's there, and it fixes the thing I patched around rather than the patch.

## What it buys

**It relocates the authority, not the capability.** Today `requires[].repo_url` lets a *plugin author* decide that installing their plugin also fetches and executes a binary from a URL of their choosing — and planning hits that URL *before* the confirmation prompt. My URL validation and unlisted-dependency warning were mitigations for that; they didn't remove it. With index-only resolution the user can still install an out-of-catalog dependency by URL manually, with a prompt, and then `install brain` sees it satisfied. The escape hatch moves from the author to the user, which is where consent belongs.

**It makes the trust model coherent.** Right now "index-listed means trusted, so no prompt" coexists with "a dependency can drag in any URL the author names." Those two rules contradict each other. Index-only resolution makes the invariant actually true: anything installed without the user typing a URL came from the curated catalog.

**It deletes code I added yesterday.** `FromIndex` becomes trivially always-true, so the unlisted-dependency annotation and its warning go. `PluginRequirement` collapses to `{name, min_version}`. `planDeps`'s URL-resolution branch loses the req-URL-vs-index-fallback distinction, and `validatePluginRepoURL` no longer needs applying to requirement URLs. That's a genuine simplification, and it's the good kind — the mitigation disappears because the hazard did.

**It gives the index a job.** With two entries and dependencies routing around it, the catalog is close to decorative. Making it the sole dependency resolver is what a curated index is actually for, and it's how krew, Homebrew and apt all behave — you can't depend on something the repository doesn't carry.

## What it costs

A dependency must be indexed before a dependent can ship. That's a real publishing-order constraint, and I think a healthy one. For internal plugin sets it means an internal index via `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` — which is exactly what that variable is now for.

The genuine loss is the long tail: someone publishing a plugin pair on their own GitHub, not in any index, can no longer express the dependency and has to document "install X first." Given they're already installing by URL with a prompt, that seems like a fair trade.

## The migration is unexpectedly clean

Because I made `entire-plugin.yml` decode leniently earlier today, dropping `repo_url` from the struct means existing published files **silently ignore it** rather than failing. So `entire-brain`'s current metadata keeps working untouched.

The only required step is adding `graph` to the index — which should happen regardless, since right now the flagship dependency flow runs entirely through URL installs with prompts. Two lines in `entireio/plugin-index`.

Worth noting the ordering that makes this work: had we kept strict decoding, this schema change would have broken every older CLI against `brain`'s published file. That's the forward-compatibility argument paying off within a day.

## One decision inside it

When a dependency is *installed but below `min_version`*, `planDeps` currently reinstalls from the recorded manifest URL rather than the index. I'd leave that alone — its provenance was already established and accepted at its own install time, and re-resolving through the index would break upgrading a dependency the user deliberately installed by URL. The index requirement should bite only when a dependency is **missing**.

Want me to implement it? It's a coordinated change: the schema and resolution here, plus adding `graph` to `entireio/plugin-index`. Implemented and pushed as `4c781ae28`. CI is running in the background; I'll report when it lands.

## What changed

`requires[]` is now `{name, min_version}` — no `repo_url`. A missing dependency resolves by name through the index and nowhere else.

**What fell out of it,** which is the satisfying part — the mitigations disappeared along with the hazard:
- `DepAction.FromIndex` is gone, and with it the per-entry `← not in the plugin index` annotation and its warning. That was code I added yesterday to make an author-chosen URL *visible*; now no such URL can appear.
- Requirement URLs no longer need validating or credential-stripping, so those code paths went too.

**One decision inside it:** the upgrade branch still reinstalls from the recorded manifest URL rather than re-resolving through the index. That provenance was established and accepted at the dependency's own install time, and re-resolving would break upgrading a dependency the user deliberately installed by URL. The index requirement bites only when a dependency is *missing*.

**The migration turned out to be free** for published files. Because `entire-plugin.yml` decodes leniently as of this morning, `entire-brain`'s existing `requires[].repo_url` is ignored rather than rejected. Had we kept strict decoding, this schema change would have broken every older CLI against that published file — the forward-compatibility argument paying for itself twice in one day.

## The one step outside this repo

`entireio/plugin-index` needs `graph` added, or `entire plugin install brain` will report the dependency as unindexed. From `entire-graph`'s own metadata:

```json
{
  "name": "graph",
  "repo_url": "https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph",
  "description": "Entity-level checkpoint context for Entire sessions"
}
```

I haven't touched that repo — it's live for every user, so that's yours to push or approve.

Two related things worth folding into the same index change:
- **`brain` isn't installable regardless.** Its v0.1.0 has a tag but no release, so there are no assets. Adding it to the index before it has a release would list a plugin that fails to install.
- **`entire-sem` and `entire-graph` have identical HEADs** (`f6783ca15`) and `sem` declares `name: graph`. If `sem` is the rename leftover it should be archived — otherwise two repos publish the same plugin, and only one of them has a basename matching its declared name.

## Still open

The two `requires[]` gaps I said were the price of keeping it: **enforcing `min_version` post-install** (the planner computes a constraint nothing downstream checks) and **`auto_installed` orphan tracking** (so `remove brain` can offer to clean up `graph`). Neither is affected by today's change — say the word and I'll do them.

From bucket 3, `browse` and `platforms` remain as Thomas's scope calls.

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a

<result>## Efficiency review: wasted work in the plugin system diff

### 1. Duplicated network work between `planDeps` and `ExecuteDepPlan` — the one finding that matters

**`cmd/entire/cli/plugin_deps.go:173,180` + `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_install_remote.go:71,99`** — dependency planning performs the exact git operations the subsequent install repeats, and throws both results away.

Per dependency that produces a `DepAction`, planning does:
- `listRemoteSemverTags` (plugin_deps.go:173) → 1 `git ls-remote --tags`
- `fetchPluginMetadataAtTag` (plugin_deps.go:180) → 1 `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none` + 1 `git show` (a separate promisor-remote blob fetch — see the comment at plugin_gitremote.go:232). On a server with `uploadpack.allowFilter` off, the filtered clone fails and a full shallow clone runs too, making it 3 git invocations.

Then `ExecuteDepPlan` (plugin_deps.go:239) → `InstallPluginFromRepo` re-runs both against the same URL, seconds later, in the same process: `listRemoteSemverTags` at plugin_install_remote.go:71 and `fetchPluginMetadataAtTag` at plugin_install_remote.go:99.

**Cost: 4 git network operations per dependency where 2 suffice.** For N=3 dependencies: 12 git operations, 6 avoidable. Each `ls-remote` is a TLS handshake plus ref advertisement (~300–800ms to a public forge); each clone+show is two fresh connections (~1–2s). That is roughly **1.5–3s of duplicate network time per dependency**, ~5–9s for a 3-dep install, on a command the user is watching.

Root cause is a data-handoff gap: `planDeps` has the resolved `tag` (line 172) and the parsed `meta` (line 180) in hand and discards both, because `DepAction` has only `Name/RepoURL/MinVersion/Upgrade/CurrentTag` — no `Tag`, no metadata.

**Cheaper alternative:** add `Tag string` and `Meta *PluginMetadata` to `DepAction`, and add a `ResolvedTag` field to `RemoteInstallOptions` that skips the `ls-remote` and the metadata clone when populated. Note `Pin` cannot be reused for this: plugin_install_remote.go:190 sets `Pinned: opts.Pin != ""`, so passing the resolved tag as `Pin` would mark every dependency pinned and make `plugin upgrade` skip it permanently.

Secondary instance of the same pattern: **plugin_install_remote.go:227 vs :71** — `UpgradeInstalledPlugin` calls `listRemoteSemverTags`, and when an upgrade actually proceeds (line 243) `InstallPluginFromRepo` calls it again. Up-to-date plugins return early at line 237 and do only one, so for `upgrade --all` over M plugins with K actually upgrading: M+K `ls-remote` where M suffices, K avoidable.

---

### 2. A full asset download issued only to be deleted

**`cmd/entire/cli/plugin_fetch.go:336-341`** — on the fallback probe path without `--allow-unverified`, the matched asset is downloaded in full via `fetchAndVerify`, then `os.Remove`d, then the function returns `errUnverifiedAsset`.

**Cost:** one complete asset transfer (the file header at line 105 says real plugin binaries are tens of MB) moved across the network purely to answer the yes/no question "does this asset exist?", then discarded. If the user then re-runs with `--allow-unverified`, the same bytes transfer a second time — **~40 MB for a 20 MB release where ~20 MB plus one metadata request would do.**

**Cheaper alternative:** probe with `HEAD` and only `GET` the winner. A 200 on `HEAD` proves existence for one RTT and zero body bytes; the `!allowUnverified` branch can then return `errUnverifiedAsset` without transferring anything, and the `allowUnverified` branch does the single `GET` it actually needs. Needs a `GET` fallback on 405/501 for hosts that don't implement `HEAD` on release assets.

Scope is honest and narrow: this only fires for releases that publish no `checksums.txt` under any of the three candidate names (plugin_fetch.go:294-319 is tried first and normally wins), which the design already discourages. But it is exactly the path the code deliberately keeps alive (comment at lines 326-330).

On the rest of the probe loop: the candidate count is 36 on darwin/arm64 (2 OS aliases × 3 arch aliases incl. `all` × 2 stem forms × 3 extensions) and 12 on linux/windows. Those are 404s on a reused keep-alive connection and the loop returns at the first hit, so **only one wasted full download occurs, not 36.** Ordering is already correct — ext-major with `darwin_arm64.tar.gz` first — so there is no win available from reordering. I would not change the candidate generation.

---

### 3. Redundant local I/O — real, O(n²)-shaped, and almost certainly not worth fixing for speed

**`cmd/entire/cli/plugin_deps.go:289-291 vs :212`** — `RunPluginDoctor` builds `installedByName` from `ListInstalledPlugins()`, then never passes it to `dependencySatisfied`, which calls `FindInstalledPlugin` → a fresh full `ListInstalledPlugins()` (1 `ReadDir` + one `Lstat` per entry) on every requirement. For M installed plugins × R requirements each: up to M·R full directory scans. At M=10, R=2: 20 `ReadDir` + ~200 `Lstat` where the map already in scope answers every query. **Cheaper: thread the map through as a parameter.**

**`plugin_deps.go:202 vs :131/:143`** — every requirement reads the dependency's `manifest.yml` twice: once inside `dependencySatisfied` (line 202), then again in `planDeps` in *both* branches (line 131 satisfied, line 143 unsatisfied). **Cheaper: have `dependencySatisfied` return the `*PluginManifest` it already loaded.**

**`plugin_deps.go:324,332`** — in doctor, the unsatisfied branch calls `LoadPluginManifest(req.Name)` at line 332 for a file `dependencySatisfied` just read at line 202. Straight-line duplicate read.

**Total manifest reads for one `plugin doctor`:** M from `ListPluginManifests` (line 310) + M·R from `dependencySatisfied` + up to M·R more from the line-332 re-read. At M=10, R=2 that is **30–50 reads + YAML parses where 10 suffice**, and since dependencies are themselves installed plugins the M·R term is O(M²) in a dense graph.

**Honest assessment: do not fix this for performance.** These are sub-kilobyte page-cached files; 40 extra reads and parses is well under a millisecond, against a doctor run whose real cost is `checkManagedBinaryIntegrity` → `fileSHA256` hashing every managed binary in full (M × tens of MB — inherent to the check, not waste). Fix it because passing the map and the loaded manifest is simpler code, not because it is slow.

**`plugin_deps.go:301,417`** — `quarantinedPath` spawns an `xattr` subprocess per installed plugin on macOS: N fork/execs at ~5–10ms each, ~50–100ms at N=10. **Cheaper: one batched `xattr -p com.apple.quarantine f1 f2 …`, or `unix.Getxattr` directly.** This is the largest avoidable cost in doctor after the SHA-256 hashing, and still imperceptible in an interactive command.

**`plugin_group.go:626 vs :165`** — `plugin browse` syncs the index, then `runRemoteInstall` syncs it again for the same URL. The second is within the TTL so there is no network hop, but it re-acquires the flock, re-reads `index.json`, re-parses the JSON, and re-runs `validatePluginName`+`validatePluginRepoURL` over every entry (~400 calls for a 200-entry catalog). Sub-millisecond. **Cheaper: pass the loaded `*PluginIndex` into `runRemoteInstall`.** Mentioned for completeness, not worth a commit on its own.

---

### 4. Sequential fan-out

**`cmd/entire/cli/plugin_group.go:479`** — `plugin upgrade --all` iterates plugins one at a time, each doing at least one `git ls-remote`. At M=10 that is 10–13 sequential network round trips, **~4–10s wall clock where a bounded `errgroup` (limit 4–8) would land near 1s.** The work is genuinely independent: distinct repos, distinct `pkg/<name>/` dirs, distinct `bin/` filenames placed by atomic rename. The only obstacle is that the per-plugin status lines are printed inline as the loop runs; buffering results and printing in name order preserves the current output exactly.

`ExecuteDepPlan` (plugin_deps.go:238) is sequential and **that is fine** — N is small, the order was shown to the user in the confirmation prompt, and dependency installs benefit from deterministic failure attribution. The `downloadPluginAsset` probe loop must stay sequential; preference order is the whole point.

---

### 5. Dispatch path and startup — clean

`cmd/entire/cli/plugin.go` is untouched by the diff (confirmed: the only changes outside the plugin_* files are a `darwinGOOS` const added in `explain.go:55` and a literal-to-const swap in `login.go:530`). `PrependPluginBinDirToPATH` (plugin_store.go:178) is unchanged. No `init()` was added in any of the seven new files. Every new code path — `SyncPluginIndex`, `ListPluginManifests`, dependency planning — sits inside a `plugin` subcommand's `RunE`. `entire <name>` dispatch remains zero-cost and no per-command startup work was added.

### 6. Closures captured into long-lived values — clean, both of them

**`plugin_fetch.go:94-102`** — `pluginHTTPClient.CheckRedirect` is package-level and long-lived, but captures **nothing**: it references only the `maxAssetRedirects` const and the package-level `requireSecureAssetURL` func. Zero retained scope. No change warranted.

**`plugin_fetch.go:269-278`** — the `assetURL` closure captures `meta` (a small `*PluginMetadata`), plus the `name`/`tag`/`repoURL` strings. It is a local variable, invoked synchronously, and never stored in a struct field, package var, or cached object — it does not outlive `downloadPluginAsset`. It also earns its keep by not duplicating the meta-vs-convention branch four times. No finding; a struct copying only the needed fields would be strictly more code for identical behavior.

One genuine (tiny) redundancy inside it: `releaseAssetBaseURL` at line 273 re-runs `url.Parse` plus string manipulation on every call, so the fallback probe loop re-derives the identical base string up to 36 times. **Cheaper: compute the base once before the loop.** This is ~20µs total, dwarfed by the 36 network round trips in the same loop — a tidiness point, not a performance one.

1. **Carry the resolved tag and metadata from `planDeps` into `ExecuteDepPlan`** (plugin_deps.go:173,180 → plugin_install_remote.go:71,99). Halves the git network operations for dependency installs: 4 per dep → 2, saving ~1.5–3s per dependency. The only finding with a user-visible number.
2. **Probe with `HEAD` in `downloadPluginAsset`'s fallback** (plugin_fetch.go:336-341). Eliminates one full tens-of-MB transfer per unverified-install rejection.
3. **Drop the duplicate `ls-remote` in `UpgradeInstalledPlugin`** (plugin_install_remote.go:227 vs :71) and **parallelize `upgrade --all`** (plugin_group.go:479). Turns a ~4–10s no-op scan into ~1s.

Its headline finding is real and quantified: **dependency planning does 4 git network operations per dependency where 2 suffice**, because `planDeps` resolves the tag and parses the metadata, discards both, and then `ExecuteDepPlan` → `InstallPluginFromRepo` re-runs `ls-remote` and the shallow clone against the same URL seconds later. It also cleared two things I'd wondered about, with reasoning I checked:
- **Both closures are fine.** `pluginHTTPClient.CheckRedirect` captures nothing — only a const and a package-level func. The `assetURL` closure is local, synchronous, never stored, and earns its keep by not duplicating the meta-vs-convention branch four times.

```go
// WriteFileAtomic writes data to filePath atomically by writing to a temp file
// in the same directory, fsyncing it, renaming into place, and fsyncing the
// parent directory. ...
// perm is applied to the temp file via Chmod before rename so the final file
// lands with the requested permission regardless of the temp file's default.
func WriteFileAtomic(filePath string, data []byte, perm fs.FileMode) error {
	dir := filepath.Dir(filePath)
	base := filepath.Base(filePath)
	tmp, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, base+".*.tmp")
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("create temp for %s: %w", filePath, err)
	}
	tmpName := tmp.Name()
	removeTmp := true
	defer func() {
		if removeTmp {
			_ = os.Remove(tmpName)
		}
	}()
	if _, err := tmp.Write(data); err != nil {
		_ = tmp.Close()
		return fmt.Errorf("write temp for %s: %w", filePath, err)
	}
	if err := tmp.Sync(); err != nil {
		_ = tmp.Close()
		return fmt.Errorf("sync temp for %s: %w", filePath, err)
	}
	if err := tmp.Close(); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("close temp for %s: %w", filePath, err)
	}
	if err := os.Chmod(tmpName, perm); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("chmod temp for %s: %w", filePath, err)
	}
	if err := os.Rename(tmpName, filePath); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("rename temp to %s: %w", filePath, err)
	}
	removeTmp = false
	// Best-effort: the rename succeeded, so don't propagate failures here. ...
	if d, err := os.Open(dir); err == nil { //nolint:gosec // G304: ...
		_ = d.Sync() //nolint:errcheck // best-effort directory fsync; ...
		_ = d.Close()
	}
	return nil
}
```

```go
func (s *reftableStorer) execGit(args ...string) (string, []byte, error) {
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), reftableGitTimeout)
	defer cancel()

	full := append([]string{"--git-dir", s.gitDir}, args...)
	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", full...)
	cmd.Env = gitPlumbingEnv()

	var stdout, stderr bytes.Buffer
	cmd.Stdout = &stdout
	cmd.Stderr = &stderr
	err := cmd.Run()
	// On our timeout the process is killed and Run reports the kill as an
	// *exec.ExitError, which would be indistinguishable from a genuine
	// non-zero exit. Re-wrap with the context error so callers (refLookupAbsent)
	// never mistake a wedged git for a definitive "ref not found".
	if err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil {
		err = fmt.Errorf("git %s timed out after %s: %w", strings.Join(args, " "), reftableGitTimeout, ctx.Err())
	}
	return strings.TrimRight(stdout.String(), "\n"), stderr.Bytes(), err
}
```

```go
// even on successful commands (shallow-clone notices, safe.directory
// advisories, etc.) and merging them would corrupt parsed output (e.g.,
// strconv.Atoi on the result of `rev-list --count` would fail).
func Run(ctx context.Context, repoRoot string, args ...string) (string, error) {
	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", args...)

	cmd.Stderr = &stderr
```

```go
// formatGitCommandError enriches an exec error from git Output() so callers see
// useful detail: context deadline expiry by name, and git's stderr (auth denied,
// repository not found, DNS) which ExitError otherwise hides behind "exit status N".
// When remote is a URL it may carry credentials that git echoes into stderr;
// those are redacted before the error is returned (same pattern as FetchBlobs).
func formatGitCommandError(ctx context.Context, err error, remote string) error {
	if err == nil {
		return nil
	}
	if errors.Is(ctx.Err(), context.DeadlineExceeded) {
		return fmt.Errorf("deadline exceeded: %w", err)
	}
	var exitErr *exec.ExitError
	if errors.As(err, &exitErr) {
		if stderr := strings.TrimSpace(string(exitErr.Stderr)); stderr != "" {
			if remote != "" {
				stderr = strings.ReplaceAll(stderr, remote, RedactURL(remote))
			}
			// Collapse whitespace so multi-line git stderr stays one log/attr value.
			stderr = strings.Join(strings.Fields(stderr), " ")
			return fmt.Errorf("%w (%s)", err, stderr)
		}
	}
	return err
}
```

```go
func splitOwnerRepo(path string) (string, string, error) {
	path = strings.TrimSuffix(path, ".git")
	parts := strings.SplitN(path, "/", 2)
	if len(parts) != 2 || parts[0] == "" || parts[1] == "" {
		return "", "", fmt.Errorf("cannot parse owner/repo from path: %s", path)
	}
	// Reject control characters (newlines, ANSI escapes, ...). The SCP-style
	// branch in ParseURL bypasses net/url.Parse's built-in control-char
	// rejection, so a crafted origin URL could otherwise smuggle a newline or
	// escape into owner/repo and, via plain-text consumers like `entire
	// agent-help`, into an agent's context or a user's terminal. This shared
	// chokepoint protects every caller; the tainted bytes are not echoed back.
	if strings.IndexFunc(parts[0]+"/"+parts[1], unicode.IsControl) >= 0 {
		return "", "", errors.New("invalid control character in remote owner/repo")
	}
	return parts[0], parts[1], nil
}
```

```go
// ParseGitHubRemote extracts owner and repo from a git remote URL that resolves
// to GitHub. It accepts direct GitHub remotes (SCP-style SSH, ssh://, and
// https://) as well as Entire mirror remotes (entire://host/gh/owner/repo),
// whose forge prefix maps back to github.com. Remotes resolving to any other
// host, or whose path holds extra segments beyond owner/repo, are rejected.
func ParseGitHubRemote(remoteURL string) (owner, repo string, err error) {
	remoteURL = strings.TrimSpace(remoteURL)
	if remoteURL == "" {
		return "", "", errors.New("empty remote URL")
	}
	info, err := gitremote.ParseURL(remoteURL)
	if err != nil {
		return "", "", fmt.Errorf("parsing remote URL: %w", err)
	}
	if host := info.CanonicalHost(); host != "github.com" {
		return "", "", fmt.Errorf("remote is not a GitHub repository (host: %s)", host)
	}
	if strings.Contains(info.Repo, "/") {
		return "", "", fmt.Errorf("remote path has extra segments beyond owner/repo: %s", gitremote.RedactURL(remoteURL))
	}
	return info.Owner, info.Repo, nil
}
```

Cleanup applied and pushed as `abf3a923f`. `mise run test:ci` green, lint 0 issues.

## Fixed

Two of these were **regressions, not tidiness** — both in code I wrote yesterday:

- **Redaction was leaking query strings.** My local `redactURL` stripped userinfo but kept the query. Release hosts redirect asset downloads to signed CDN URLs, so `?token=` / `X-Amz-Signature=` would have reached error messages — and my "credentials never leak" test passed anyway because it only tested userinfo. Now delegates to `gitremote.RedactURL`, the repo-wide helper that already strips both. **Five call sites had also been missed**, including both of `validatePluginRepoURL`'s own rejection messages, which echo the URL being rejected.

The rest were genuine cleanups: `dependencySatisfied` returns the manifest it loaded (three reads per requirement → one, two duplicated blocks gone); `downloadPluginAsset` resolves the URL prefix once instead of re-parsing per candidate and carrying an error return through three call sites; `--index` collapsed from five registrations to one helper; the duplicated index sync hoisted out of both branches; and the integration fixture's stale `requires[].repo_url` now points at an unreachable host so it proves the ignore path instead of implying the field still works.

**Behavior risk:** carrying the resolved tag from `planDeps` into the install (would suppress the tag-fallback walk for pushed-but-unpublished releases — the biggest efficiency win at ~1.5–3s per dependency, but not a cleanup); `HEAD`-probing before download (needs a 405 fallback); parallelizing `upgrade --all` (adds an errgroup to a rare command).

**Outside the diff:** promoting `silencePluginCancel` to `errors.go` and collapsing the three other copies; adding a redaction pass at `main.go`'s print boundary — this one is the strongest remaining idea, because `%w`-wrapped `url.Error` leaks the full credentialed URL no matter how disciplined the call sites are, and one line there would cover every site including future ones. I did fix the comment that cited `activity_cmd.go` as precedent; that file contains no such pattern.

**Wants your call:** splitting `InstallPluginFromRepo` into `InstallKnownPlugin` / `InstallPluginFromURL` so `ExpectedName` can't be forgotten. Sound argument — an optional field guards a no-prompt install path — but it's a public API shape change I'd rather Thomas weighed in on.

**Largest remaining item:** ~215 lines of test-helper duplication. Two near-identical release servers, four repo-fixture builders, two tar.gz writers, and a 4-line preamble repeated eight times. So the duplication is entirely self-inflicted by this branch, not shared with pre-existing tests. My "reaches outside the diff" justification was wrong for the bulk of it.

**What's actually in scope.** Six of the seven files are `package cli`, so they can be deduped among themselves touching nothing pre-existing — roughly 140–150 of the ~215 lines:

- `updateRepoMetadata` (15 lines of hand-rolled `git add` + `git -c user.name=… commit`) when the *same file* already does that correctly in 5 lines with `testutil.WriteFile`/`GitAdd`/`GitCommit`
- the `srv` + `defer Close` + `meta` + `repoURL` preamble repeated 8× (~32 lines), with the `download_url` format string written 10 times
- ~6 of the 13 ad-hoc `httptest` servers in `plugin_fetch_test.go`, two of which are byte-identical pairs
- `withPluginDir` + `withIsolatedPath` always paired, 20 times
- `t.Setenv("XDG_CACHE_HOME", t.TempDir())` 8 times
- direct `os.WriteFile`/`os.MkdirAll` where pre-existing `testutil.WriteFile` already creates parents

That last group is *using* pre-existing helpers more, not changing them — which is the opposite of reaching outside the diff.

**What genuinely does reach outside** is only the unit↔integration sharing, ~65–75 lines: `pluginReleaseServer` vs `startReleaseServer` (18 lines byte-identical), `newTaggedPluginRepo` vs `newPluginRepo`, the two `newIndexRepo`s with the same name and different signatures, and `makeTarGz` vs `makeScriptTarGz`. Unexported `_test.go` helpers can't cross packages, so those need a home in `testutil` — a shared package many other suites depend on.

There's also one real correctness angle hiding in here, which is why I'd not leave it all: the three `git tag` shell-outs and the bare-repo init set no `cmd.Env`, so they inherit the developer's global git config. A developer with `tag.gpgSign=true` would see those tests fail locally. The pre-existing `testutil.CreateBranch` and `GitReset` handle this by passing `GitIsolatedEnv()` per command — the new helpers just didn't follow the pattern.

My suggestion: do the in-package portion now, since it's squarely the changed code, and add the `GitIsolatedEnv()` to the tag/bare-init shell-outs while I'm there. Leave the cross-package `testutil` consolidation as a separate call — it's a shared-package change that's worth doing only if that release-server logic drifts again, and it'd be cleaner as its own commit.

Done — `143c652c5`. Full CI green, lint 0 issues.

To answer the question directly: **only one of the three was in scope.** I checked rather than assumed:

- `main.go` — pre-existing, not in the diff
- `errors.go`, `session_tokens.go`, `authcmd.go`, `clean.go` — all pre-existing, so consolidating `silencePluginCancel` means editing files this PR never touched

So I did the third.

## What changed

`RemoteInstallOptions` carried `RepoURL` and `ExpectedName` as fields. Neither is an option — one is the target, the other is a security decision. Both are now required arguments:

```go
InstallPluginFromRepo(ctx, repoURL, expectedName string, opts RemoteInstallOptions)
```

The struct is down to the three genuine options: `Pin`, `Force`, `AllowUnverified`.

The point isn't cosmetic. `ExpectedName` as a field could be silently omitted, and omitting it reopens the hole it exists to close — an index entry named `safe` installing `entire-hijack`, or `--force` on plugin A replacing an unrelated installed B. And no test can catch a field missing from a caller that doesn't exist yet. As an argument, `""` is still expressible but it's a visible choice rather than an omission.

## Where I didn't follow the reviewer

The altitude agent wanted two functions — `InstallKnownPlugin` and `InstallPluginFromURL` — so the compiler forces the choice. I didn't, and the reason is specific: two of three callers always know the name, but `runRemoteInstall` legitimately handles both cases. Splitting would move the `""` into a branch there rather than eliminate it, so you'd get the same residual expressiveness for twice the exported surface. I noted that trade in the commit so the next reader doesn't re-derive it.

## Remaining, both genuinely out of scope

The `main.go` print-boundary redaction is still the strongest idea from the whole `/simplify` pass, and worth flagging to Thomas for a follow-up: `%w`-wrapped `url.Error` prints the full credentialed URL regardless of how disciplined the call sites are, because `net/url.Error.Error()` does no redaction. One line at `main.go`'s error print would cover every current site, the five I'd missed, and every future one. It's a global change to error output, so it wants its own PR and its own thought about what else it might scrub.

The `silencePluginCancel` promotion is lower value — four copies of a 3-line convention, where the newest (mine) is the best of them because of the `ctx.Err()` check the other three lack. Also a follow-up on pre-existing files.

Solution: Added a plugin system that discovers, installs, upgrades, and manages plugins from configurable git-synced indexes. input.content:
## Summary

Expands the kubectl-style external-command layer so users can discover and install plugins without cloning anything, from any git host. 18 files, ~5,540 insertions.

- **Remote install** — `entire plugin install <name|url|path>`. Newest **stable** semver tag via `git ls-remote` (forge-agnostic, inherits git auth and proxies; no forge REST client anywhere). Optional `entire-plugin.yml` metadata read via blobless shallow clone. Release assets download over HTTPS through a small per-host URL convention table (GitHub/Gitea-style, GitLab-style, `download_url` template escape hatch), selected and verified against the release's `checksums.txt`. Binaries land in `pkg/<name>/` with a provenance `manifest.yml`; `bin/` stays the only dispatch surface and the resolver in `plugin.go` is untouched.
- **Upgrade** — `entire plugin upgrade [name|--all]`, `--pin` to hold a tag, next-highest-tag fallback for pushed-but-unpublished releases, Windows locked-binary rename-aside.
- **Discovery** — krew-style git-synced index ([entireio/plugin-index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index)): shallow-cloned into the user cache keyed by URL hash, flock-guarded, 24h TTL, stale-copy-on-offline. New `search`/`info`/`browse`/`index update` subcommands; bare-name installs resolve through the index. Index URL: `--index` > `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` > built-in default.
- **Dependencies** — `entire-plugin.yml` `requires` (`name` + optional `min_version`, no ranges), resolved by name through the index. Install-time transitive planning, apt-style single confirmation, remove guard for depended-on plugins, and `entire plugin doctor`. Dispatch stays zero-cost — no runtime dependency checks.

## Security model

This code ends in downloading a binary and making it executable, so the trust boundaries are the design:

- **Transport.** HTTPS required for anything off-machine, re-validated on every redirect hop (Go follows redirects across schemes; validating only the entry point is bypassable). Loopback exempt so `httptest` fixtures work.
- **Authentication.** A release that publishes no `checksums.txt` for the platform is **refused by default**; `--allow-unverified` opts in, is recorded in the manifest, reported by `doctor`, and inherited by `upgrade`.
- **Integrity.** The installed binary's digest is recorded as `binary_sha256` and re-checked by `doctor`. (`sha256` covers the downloaded *asset*, which is discarded with the staging dir — provenance only.)
- **URLs reaching git.** Every repo/index URL is scheme-validated by one definition and every git invocation passes `--` before positionals. Repo URLs are attacker-influenced (index entries, `--index`, env), and git reads an option-shaped positional as an option — `--upload-pack`'s value is shell-interpreted.
- **The trust root is not repo-choosable.** The index URL cannot be set from committed settings; see below.
- **Names.** The installed name comes from the remote, so callers that already committed to a name pass it as a required argument and a mismatch is fatal.
- **Credentials.** Userinfo and query strings are stripped from every URL before printing, logging, or persisting (`.entire/logs/` is inside the working tree and `doctor bundle` collects it wholesale; `manifest.yml` is mode 0644).

Not claimed: **authenticity**. `checksums.txt` shares an origin with the asset, so it proves integrity in transit, not publisher identity. Real authenticity needs signatures.

## Design notes

- Built on the recorded founding decisions of this layer: PATH dispatch unchanged, built-ins win, `agent-` prefix reserved, env filtering untouched, no new telemetry.
- The only forge-specific code is the download-URL convention table; version listing, metadata, and the index all ride on the git protocol. No `go-github`-class dependency (uses existing `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` + `golang.org/x/mod`).
- **The plugin layer reads no settings at all.** The `settings` package is byte-identical to `main`.

## Changed since this description was first written

The branch was reviewed (Bugbot ×5 rounds, Copilot, four trail agent reviews, and a three-agent adversarial pass), then merged with `main` (2053 commits). Reviewers should know these are new:

**Behavior changes**
1. Checksums are now **required** by default (`--allow-unverified` opts out). Previously a release without them installed silently.
2. `http://` and `git://` are no longer accepted for repo or index URLs — unauthenticated transports, and the catalog decides what installs without a prompt.
3. Prereleases are excluded from tag resolution. `v2.0.0-rc1` outranks stable `v1.9.0` in semver, so `upgrade --all` was migrating users onto release candidates.

**Removals**
4. **`plugins.index_url` and `plugins.index_ttl_hours` are gone.** `.entire/settings.json` is committed and resolved from the working directory, while an index-listed plugin installs with *no prompt* — so a cloned repo could redirect the catalog and get an attacker-chosen binary onto `PATH` silently. The setting's value was that contributors got a different catalog *without knowing*, which is the vulnerability stated as a feature. Internal catalogs now use `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`, which applies across repos and cannot be chosen by checked-out content. Go takes the same position with `GOPROXY`; npm's per-project registry is the cautionary counter-example.
5. **`requires[].repo_url` is gone.** Dependencies resolve by name through the index, so a dependency's URL comes from the curated catalog rather than the requiring plugin's author — planning contacted that URL *before* the confirmation prompt. A user can still install an out-of-catalog dependency themselves, with the usual prompt; the authority moved to the user.

**Fixes worth naming**
6. Argument injection into the git CLI allowing arbitrary command execution from a malicious index entry or dependency URL — verified live on the pre-fix tree, on a path that never prompts.
7. `entire-plugin.yml` now decodes **leniently**. Strict decoding meant the first author to adopt any future field would break installs on every older CLI, permanently. This is also what made removals 4 and 5 migration-free for already-published files.
8. Silent truncation of archive entries over 512 MiB, index-cache races (now flock-guarded), a diamond `min_version` skip, `darwin_all` universal binaries never matching, empty `entire-plugin.yml` being fatal, `index_ttl_hours` overflowing to "always stale", and credential leaks through download errors.

## Testing

- ~60 unit tests against `file://` git repos and `httptest` asset servers (zero real network in CI), covering tag resolution, asset selection/verification, extraction guards, index sync/TTL/offline/concurrency, dependency planning, doctor.
- 4 integration tests drive the spawned binary end to end: bare-name install → real dispatch → dependency install → remove guard → doctor exit code. They run the **verified** path — no test passes `--allow-unverified`, so their passing is the proof that verification succeeds.
- Security regressions assert the stronger property where it matters: that an injected payload never executes and that credentials never appear, not merely that a call errors. Each was verified RED against the pre-fix tree.
- `mise run check` green (fmt, lint, unit + integration + Vogon canary).

## Docs

- `docs/architecture/external-commands.md` — remote install, plugin index, dependencies, and the trust-boundary sections.
- README — user-facing Plugins section.

## Open, deliberately

- `browse` and `index.json`'s `platforms` are candidates to cut — `browse` adds no capability over `search` + `install` and installs unprompted; `platforms` warns but never enforces.
- `min_version` is not enforced on the install *outcome* (the planner computes a constraint nothing downstream checks), and dependencies have no `auto_installed` marker, so orphans leak.
- Two notions of "official": the `officialPlugins` telemetry allowlist and `index.json`'s `official` flag.
- `entire upgrade` (the self-update plugin) vs `entire plugin upgrade` (plugins).
- Follow-up outside this branch: a credential-redaction pass at `main.go`'s error print. `%w`-wrapped `url.Error` leaks the full URL regardless of call-site discipline, because `net/url.Error.Error()` does no redaction.
- Outside this repo: `graph` should be added to `entireio/plugin-index`, or `entire plugin install brain` reports its dependency as unindexed.

Problem: The CLI had no way to extend its functionality with community or organizational plugins. The system needed to safely distribute and manage executable plugins from remote sources while defending against supply-chain attacks.

Solution: Added a plugin system that discovers, installs, upgrades, and manages plugins from a git-synced index. Remote plugins resolve the newest stable semver tag over git (prereleases require an explicit --pin), download release assets over HTTPS with the transport re-validated on every redirect hop, and verify them against the checksums.txt published alongside the release. Unauthenticated downloads are refused by default unless --allow-unverified is passed; verification status is recorded in the install manifest, reported by doctor, and inherited on upgrade. Installed binaries are digested at install time and re-checked by `entire plugin doctor` to detect tampering.

Trust boundaries are the design, because the code path ends in making a downloaded file executable. Every repository and index URL is scheme-validated by a single definition and every git invocation passes `--` before its positionals, since git reads an option-shaped positional as an option and --upload-pack's value is shell-interpreted. The installed plugin name comes from the remote, so callers that have already committed to a name pass it as a required argument and a mismatch is fatal. Credentials and query strings are stripped from every URL before it is printed, logged, or persisted.

Two things are deliberately NOT configurable, both because the alternative was exploitable. The index URL cannot be set from committed repo settings: .entire/settings.json is resolved from the working directory while an index-listed plugin installs with no prompt, so a cloned repository could have redirected the catalog and put an attacker-chosen binary on PATH silently. Internal catalogs use ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL instead, which applies across repositories and cannot be chosen by checked-out content. Likewise a dependency carries no repo_url: requires[] is name plus an optional min_version, resolved through the index, so a dependency's download URL comes from the curated catalog rather than from the requiring plugin's author. The plugin layer reads no settings at all.

Authenticity is explicitly not claimed. checksums.txt shares an origin with the asset it describes, so it proves integrity in transit, not publisher identity; that would need signatures.

Coverage: 77 unit tests against file:// git repos and httptest servers with zero real network, plus 4 integration tests driving the spawned binary end to end through install, dispatch, dependency resolution, the remove guard, and doctor's exit code. The integration tests run the verified path — none passes --allow-unverified, so their passing is what proves verification succeeds. Security regressions assert that an injected payload never executes and that credentials never appear, rather than merely that a call errors, and each was verified failing against the pre-fix tree.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

content.text:
Real bug, and mine. Fixed in `f4a5f206c` — CI green, lint 0 issues, finding resolved.

## What it was

`classifyInstallArg` tested for a literal `git@` prefix, while the `scpLikeGitURL` regex I added later accepts **any** SSH username. Two definitions of "scp-like git URL" that disagreed — and since the broader one came second, the classifier was the one left behind.

Anyone whose forge uses a non-default user hit this. Verified against the built binary before touching anything:

```
git@git.corp.io:group/entire-foo.git      → list tags of git@... : git ls-remote   ✓ routed to the repo
deploy@git.corp.io:group/entire-foo.git   → stat source: stat /tmp/deploy@git.corp.io:group/entire-foo.git:
                                             no such file or directory              ✗ routed to the filesystem
```

The second form is one my own validator would have happily installed from — the classifier just never let it get there. `deploy@`, `ci-bot@`, `forge-user@` are all ordinary in corporate SSH setups.

## The fix

`classifyInstallArg` now uses `scpLikeGitURL`, so there's one definition. The scp-like test has to run **before** the separator test, because these URLs contain a `/` too — which is exactly why the old ordering worked for `git@` (caught by the prefix check first) and failed for everything else.

After:
```
git@git.corp.io:...      → git ls-remote   ✓
deploy@git.corp.io:...   → git ls-remote   ✓
./entire-localdemo       → Installed plugin "localdemo" → …/bin/entire-localdemo   ✓
```

Test cases cover a non-default username, a hyphenated one, and `./deploy@host:x` — which stays a *path*, because the regex anchors the username at the start.

## Why this one is worth noting

It's the second finding of exactly this shape: I broadened a definition and left its twin behind. The first was `validatePluginRepoURL` vs `PluginSettings.Validate` disagreeing on `http://`/`git://`/absolute paths, which `/simplify` caught. Both times the fix was "one definition, shared" — and both times the drift came from *my* change rather than the original code.

Worth telling Thomas as a pattern, not just two bugs: `scpLikeGitURL` is now referenced from two places, so the next person to touch it should check both. There's an argument for the classifier and the validator living next to each other rather than in `plugin_group.go` and `plugin_gitremote.go`, though I'd leave that call to him.

The gates now read **Checks ✅ / Findings ✅**, with only the human-approval gate outstanding.

content.text:
Two things worth knowing before I answer:

```
classifyInstallArg    defined plugin_group.go
validatePluginRepoURL defined plugin_gitremote.go   used in 3 files
scpLikeGitURL         defined plugin_gitremote.go   used in 2 files
normalizeRepoURL      defined plugin_index.go
pluginNameFromRepoURL defined plugin_gitremote.go
releaseAssetBaseURL   defined plugin_fetch.go
```

The source-URL vocabulary is spread across **four** files, not two. And more importantly:

```
133:  if classifyInstallArg(arg) == installFromPath  { ... }   ← install RunE
182:  if classifyInstallArg(arg) == installFromIndex { ... }   ← runRemoteInstall
```

**The argument is classified twice.** That's the actual structural problem, and it's why the drift was easy to miss — the decision isn't made once and carried, it's re-derived from a raw string at each point of use. Co-locating files wouldn't have prevented it.

## What I'd suggest

**Make it one decision, not two.** A `parseInstallSource` that classifies *and* validates in a single pass, called once at the command boundary, with a typed result passed down:

```go
type installSource struct {
    Kind installArgKind
    // Ref is the repository URL, the filesystem path, or the catalog name,
    // according to Kind.
    Ref string
}

func parseInstallSource(arg string) (installSource, error) {
    switch {
    case strings.Contains(arg, "://") || scpLikeGitURL.MatchString(arg):
        return installSource{installFromURL, arg}, validatePluginRepoURL(arg)
    case strings.ContainsAny(arg, `/\`) || strings.HasPrefix(arg, "."):
        return installSource{installFromPath, arg}, nil
    default:

}
```

- **Classification and validation can't disagree** — they're the same function. The bug I just fixed becomes unrepresentable rather than merely commented.
- **The arg is classified once.** `runRemoteInstall` takes a typed source instead of re-deriving from a string.
- **It's a free error-message upgrade.** A bare name currently goes to the index and comes back "not in the index"; validating at the boundary means `agent-foo` says "reserved prefix" and a name with a separator says so, instead of blaming the catalog.

Cost is small — one type, one function, two call sites rewired, all in files already in the diff. And the justification isn't aesthetic: this exact 3-way switch has already drifted once and is already evaluated twice.

That's a coherent unit — "what is a plugin source, and what can you ask about one" — and it leaves `plugin_gitremote.go` as what its name says: the git shell-outs. But this is secondary. Co-location makes the next drift *visible*; the single decision makes it *impossible*. Do the second first.

**What I would not move:** `releaseAssetBaseURL` and `requireSecureAssetURL` stay in `plugin_fetch.go`. They're about asset URLs and download transport, a genuinely different concern from "what did the user ask to install."

You could argue a type and a function is heavy for a three-way switch on a string. I don't think so here, but the reason is empirical rather than principled: it drifted once already, and it's computed twice. Absent that evidence I'd have left it alone.

Done — `32991c49a`. Full CI green, lint 0 issues.

## What landed

`parseInstallSource(arg) (installSource, error)` classifies and validates in one pass, called once at the command boundary. `runRemoteInstall` now takes a typed `installSource` instead of re-deriving the kind from a raw string.

Three things fell out of it:

**The drift is now unrepresentable.** One function can't disagree with itself. Sharing the regex fixed the bug; this removes the shape that produced it.

**The argument is classified once.** It was being classified twice — once in the install command to split off the path case, once in `runRemoteInstall` for the index case.

**Better errors, for free.** `entire plugin install agent-evil` now says `plugin name "agent-evil" is reserved for the external agent protocol` instead of going to the catalog and coming back "not in the index".

I also added a leading-`-` rejection for every kind. Previously `--upload-pack=touch /tmp/x; git-upload-pack` contained a separator, so it went down the *path* branch and failed as `stat: no such file` — safe, but a confusing way to say "that's not a plugin."

## Two things my own test got wrong

Worth recording, because the failures were informative rather than annoying. I wrote expectations that `--upload-pack=…` and `ext::sh -c whoami` would be rejected as URLs. Neither was:

- `--upload-pack=…` contains `/`, so it was a *path*
- `ext::sh -c whoami` has no separator and no scheme, so it was an *index name* — and `validatePluginName` permits spaces and colons

The code was right and my mental model was wrong. Both stop well before git sees a repository URL, which is the property that actually matters. I fixed the expectations rather than the code, and left a comment recording why those two shapes are deliberately accepted — otherwise the next person reads the gap as an oversight and "fixes" it.

I did **not** tighten `validatePluginName` to reject spaces and colons. It's pre-existing, it also governs local installs, and the looseness is harmless on the two routes that reach it.

## The file-layout half

Not done, deliberately, and the commit message says so. The source vocabulary is spread over four files — validator and scp regex in `plugin_gitremote.go`, the parser in `plugin_group.go`, `normalizeRepoURL` in `plugin_index.go`, asset URLs in `plugin_fetch.go`. Co-location would make a future drift *visible*; one decision makes it *impossible*. Having done the second, the first is now optional taste rather than risk mitigation — which is why it's a reasonable thing to leave to Thomas rather than something I should have pushed through.

content.text:
Both were still relevant, and both real. Fixed in `653eced31` — full CI green, lint 0 issues, both resolved.

## The seven older findings

All show `resolved / stale`. Stale means the code they point at has since moved — expected after this many refactors, and no action needed. Nothing was reintroduced.

## The two new ones

**Manifest inconsistent with the binary** (`plugin_install_remote.go:169`). Verified the ordering: `replaceBinary` ran, then `fileSHA256`, `InstallPluginFromPath`, and `SavePluginManifest` — three fallible steps *after* the binary was already swapped. A failure or Ctrl+C in any of them left the new binary on disk against the old recorded tag and digest, which `checkManagedBinaryIntegrity` reads as *"modified or replaced outside entire"*.

That's the worst kind of bug in a security feature: a **permanent false tampering alarm on a healthy install**. It teaches users to ignore the alarm.

The manifest now writes immediately after the swap, before the `bin/` link, leaving only a local re-hash in the window. And the residual failure mode became an accurate one — if the link fails, doctor says *"has an install manifest but no entry in the managed bin dir"* with a fix that works. `SavePluginManifest` also goes through `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic` now, which closes the reuse finding from `/simplify` at the same time.

**Dependency outcome unverified** (`plugin_deps.go:249`). `ExecuteDepPlan` installed the newest published tag and never checked it against the plan's `min_version`, so if a dependency hadn't cut a qualifying release it printed "Installed dependency" while the requirement stayed unmet. It now fails with both versions named.

This is the item that had been sitting on the knowingly-open list since the dependency system was first reviewed — I'd flagged it three times as "the price of keeping `requires[]`". It's now paid. The check runs *after* the install deliberately, so the dependency stays on disk at the too-old version and doctor reports `requires demo >= v9.0.0 but v0.1.0 is installed` — accurate and actionable, rather than leaving nothing to diagnose.

## Two bugs in my own tests, worth noting

Both first drafts failed for reasons that were about my tests, not the code:

- The dependency test's second case hit `already installed; use --force` — because the *first* case's install succeeds before the min-version check rejects it. That's the behavior I'd just designed, and I'd forgotten it one line later. Fixed with `Upgrade: true`, and I added an assertion documenting that the too-old version is deliberately left installed.
- The upgrade test called `updateRepoMetadata` with content identical to what was already committed → `cannot create empty commit`. A new tag on the same commit was all it needed.

Both are the kind of thing that would have been a confusing CI failure for someone else, so I'd rather they surfaced here.

## Remaining open

From the earlier reviews, all still open and all deliberate: `browse` and `platforms` as cut candidates, `auto_installed` orphan tracking, the two notions of "official", `entire upgrade` naming, the `main.go` redaction follow-up, and adding `graph` to the published index.

The min-version item has dropped off that list. Gates should read **Checks ✅ / Findings ✅** once CI finishes on this head.
