content.text:
Both are small pieces of the discovery surface.

## `entire plugin browse`

An interactive picker over the catalog. It syncs the index, builds a `huh` select list of every entry as `name — description` plus a `(cancel)` option, and on selection calls `runRemoteInstall` with the chosen name.

```
$ entire plugin browse
? Install a plugin
  > run — Launch one of the agents enabled for Entire in the current repository
    upgrade — Upgrade the system-installed entire binary
    (cancel)
```

It needs a TTY — without one it errors and points at `search`.

**Why it's a cut candidate:** it's `search` + `install` with arrow keys, and it installs on **one keypress with no confirmation**. Index-resolved installs are treated as trusted and never prompt, so the select list *is* the confirmation — Enter on a highlighted row downloads a binary and puts it on your `PATH`. `search` then `install <name>` is two commands, but the second is a deliberate act. Combined with a catalog that currently has two entries, it's the piece I'd cut with least hesitation.

## `platforms` in `index.json`

An optional per-entry list of GOOS values — "supported platforms when the plugin doesn't ship the full matrix; empty means all":

```json
{"name": "run", "repo_url": "...", "platforms": ["darwin", "linux"]}
```

It's read in exactly two places. `plugin info` displays it, and on install it produces a warning that changes nothing:

```go
if len(entry.Platforms) > 0 && !slices.Contains(entry.Platforms, runtime.GOOS) {
    fmt.Fprintf(errOut, "Warning: index lists %q for %s only; this is %s — continuing anyway.\n", ...)
}
```

**Why it's a cut candidate — two reasons, and the second is the real one:**

It enforces nothing. If the platform genuinely isn't published, the download fails on its own a moment later with `no matching release asset for windows/amd64 at <repo> <tag>` — which is more accurate, since it reflects what was *actually* published rather than what the catalog claims.

And it lives in the wrong artifact. The **author** knows their build matrix; the **catalog** is a third party describing someone else's release. So it drifts in the direction that hurts: an author adds Windows support, the catalog entry still says `["darwin","linux"]`, and the CLI now warns about a plugin that works perfectly. A stale "this won't work" is worse than no claim at all.

If you wanted the capability, the right home is `entire-plugin.yml` alongside `download_url`, where it can't drift from the release. Even there it'd be largely redundant with asset probing.

## My recommendation on each

**`platforms`** — cut. There's no version of this that earns its place in the catalog, and the honest signal already exists in the download failure.

**`browse`** — cut, or keep it and add a confirmation. The no-prompt install is the part I'd object to more than the redundancy; a picker that shows the repo URL and asks before installing would be defensible. But given `search` already prints everything the picker shows, cutting is simpler.

Both are Thomas's calls — they're features he built, and neither is broken. They're "this costs more than it earns" arguments, not defect reports, which is why I've kept them on the list rather than acting on them.

content.text:
Added in `fb8412b57`. Full CI green, lint 0 issues.

## What browse does now

```
$ entire plugin browse
? Install a plugin
  > run — Launch one of the agents enabled for Entire in the current repository
    upgrade — Upgrade the system-installed entire binary
    (cancel)

? Install "run" from https://github.com/entireio/entire-run?   ← new
```

The confirmation names **the repository**, which is the fact the picker hides — it only ever showed name and description. That's the substantive part: previously you could arrow to a row, press Enter, and a binary from a URL you'd never seen was downloaded and linked onto your `PATH`.

It follows the same `handleFormCancellation` convention as the untrusted-URL prompt, so Esc and "No" both exit cleanly with `Install cancelled.` rather than differing by exit code.

I also gave browse a `Long` description — it had only a one-line `Short` — stating that it needs a terminal and pointing at `search` + `install <name>`. That's the non-interactive equivalent the repo's agent-safe-fallback rule requires, and it was already the behavior; it just wasn't documented.

## On the test

Worth being straight about the limit: the interactive prompt itself isn't unit-testable without a TTY harness. Under `go test`, `CanPromptInteractively()` is false, so browse returns at its terminal check before the confirm is reachable.

So the test covers the documented no-terminal path and asserts the error names the alternative. That's the same coverage shape the untrusted-URL prompt has — `TestPluginRemoteInstall_URLNeedsYesWhenUnlisted` tests the non-interactive gate, not the prompt. I followed the existing pattern rather than inventing a harness for one call site, but the confirm logic itself is unexercised, and that's a real gap rather than something I've covered.

## What this does and doesn't settle

It closes the part I actually objected to. The unprompted install was the security-shaped complaint; redundancy with `search` + `install` is just cost.

The larger question stays open and is Thomas's: `browse` is still an interactive-only picker over a two-entry catalog that does what two other commands already do. With a confirmation it's now *defensible* rather than something I'd argue against — which is a better position to leave it in for someone else to decide.

`platforms` is untouched. Unlike browse there's no version of it I'd defend: it enforces nothing, and it lives in the catalog rather than with the author, so it drifts toward warning about plugins that work fine.

Here's the answer to both halves:

## PR comments — nothing new

The last comment is my own from Aug 5. No new bot reviews (Bugbot hasn't re-run), and **all 13 review threads are resolved**. Nothing is waiting on you there.

## Trail — one new Low finding, now fixed (`ab61a0b7e`)

`ParsePluginMetadata` validated each requirement's `name` but not its `min_version`. I verified the mechanism before touching it:

```
min="v0.2.0"  valid=true   Compare(v1.0.0,min)= 1  satisfied=true
min="vtypo"   valid=false  Compare(v1.0.0,min)= 1  satisfied=true   ←
min="latest"  valid=false  Compare(v1.0.0,min)= 1  satisfied=true   ←
min=">=1.0"   valid=false  Compare(v1.0.0,min)= 1  satisfied=true   ←
```

`x/mod/semver` ranks an invalid string below *every* valid one, so a typo doesn't fail — it makes the comparison always true and the version floor **silently disappears**. Low severity is right (it needs an author typo, and it weakens rather than breaks), but it's the worst failure direction for a guarantee: you'd believe the minimum was enforced when nothing was checking it.

The likeliest mistake is range syntax, since the field is deliberately a minimum only — and `>=1.0` is precisely one of the shapes that disabled the check. It now gets an explicit "minimum only — ranges are not supported."

## One thing I want to flag about this fix

It looks like it contradicts a decision I made earlier today. This morning I made `entire-plugin.yml` decode **leniently** and argued that author-side validation belongs in a lint command, not in every user's install path. Now I'm adding author-side validation to that same function.

The distinction is real, and I put it in the code comment so the next reader doesn't see a contradiction:

- **Unknown keys stay lenient** — they're a *newer CLI's fields*. Refusing them breaks older binaries permanently, for everyone on that version, with no way for the author to fix it.
- **A malformed value of a known field is strict** — no CLI version will ever accept `latest` as a semver tag. Rejecting it costs the author one confused test run.

And the precedent was already there: `req.Name` is validated in the very same loop. So this is consistent with that function's existing behavior, not a new policy.

All three verified against the code. Here's what I think.

## They're all real, and the High one is the most serious finding since the git injection

**`--force` on a bare URL install can replace a different plugin** — this is a genuine escalation and I'd fix it before anything else.

The guard reads `if expectedName != "" && name != expectedName`. On a bare `install <url>`, `expectedName` is empty by design, so it's skipped entirely — and then `existing != nil && !opts.Force` lets `--force` overwrite whatever the *remote's* `entire-plugin.yml` names. You confirm "Install from `https://github.com/someone/entire-foo`?" and their metadata says `name: ci`, so your installed `entire-ci` is replaced.

The reason it's more than theoretical: **install doesn't execute the binary**. So at install time the attacker hasn't run anything — the payoff is that the *next* `entire ci` runs their code instead. You consented to fetching plugin "foo" and got a different, already-trusted plugin swapped underneath you.

What makes it worse is the second finding's observation: **`plugin doctor` actively teaches this shape**. Three of its Fix strings say `entire plugin install <repo-url> --force`. So the muscle memory the tool builds is exactly the dangerous invocation.

I'd take the suggested fix — when `expectedName` is empty and `--force` would replace an existing install, require the existing manifest's `RepoURL` to normalize to the same repo, else refuse and name the plugin that would be replaced. That preserves the legitimate case (reinstalling the same plugin from the same repo, which is what doctor suggests) and blocks the cross-plugin swap. One judgment call inside it: a *local-dev* install has no manifest to compare, and I'd let that be replaced rather than break "swap my dev build for the real one."

## The other two are smaller but both make the tool lie

**Nil index on a URL install** — when `SyncPluginIndex` fails, `idx` is nil, and it's still handed to dependency planning. `Find` returns nil on a nil receiver, so you get *"dependency X is not installed and is not in the plugin index"* when the truth is the catalog never loaded. That fails the command with a non-zero exit **after** the plugin installed and printed its success line — which directly contradicts the contract written four lines below the call site: *"a declined or non-confirmable plan degrades to a warning, not an error."*

**Doctor's reinstall can't work on the plugins it flags** — for a plugin installed with `--allow-unverified`, `install <url> --force` re-runs with verification required and fails. Doctor exits 1 and hands you a command that cannot succeed. Fix is appending `--allow-unverified` to those three strings when `m.Unverified`.

Both are the same species of defect: correct-looking output that misdirects the user. Neither is dangerous, both are cheap.

## What I actually think about the pattern

Six review rounds in, and this round found a High. That's worth noticing rather than dismissing — I'd assumed the surface was thinning, and it wasn't.

Two of these three trace to my own recent changes: `ExpectedName` closed the name hole on three paths and left the fourth open, and the min-version/index work made dependencies index-only without handling a nil index. The `--force` gap in particular is the *same* escalation my `161a73b30` commit claimed to close — I fixed three callers and didn't ask what the fourth did. That's the second time in this session I've broadened a definition and left a sibling behind.

This round's findings are also `whole_change`-scoped rather than line-scoped, which is why they caught interactions across files that the incremental passes didn't.

My recommendation: fix all three — the High for the escalation, and the two Mediums because they're a handful of lines each and both currently produce misleading output. Want me to?

content.text:
## When doctor suggests `--force`

Three cases, all in `checkManagedBinaryIntegrity` and the manifest loop:

| Problem | Suggested fix |
|---|---|
| has an install manifest but no entry in the managed bin dir | `install <url> --force` |
| managed binary is missing or unreadable | `install <url> --force` |
| managed binary no longer matches the recorded digest | `install <url> --force` |

All three are **repair**: something under the managed dir got broken, deleted, or modified, and the way back is to fetch it again. `--force` is needed purely because a record of the plugin still exists, so a plain `install` would refuse with "already installed."

And the crucial detail: `<url>` is `m.RepoURL` — **the manifest of the plugin being repaired**. So doctor always says "reinstall *this* plugin from where *it* came from." The repo matches by construction.

## Which means my proposed fix was wrong

You're right that `--force` is exactly for "overwrite what's there." And a repo-mismatch refusal would break a case you have live right now: `entire-sem` and `entire-graph` are the same plugin at the same commit, with `sem` declaring `name: graph`. Someone moving `graph` from the old repo to the new one is doing something entirely legitimate, and my guard would have blocked it.

The defect isn't that `--force` replaces things. It's that **the confirmation names a URL and never says which installed plugin it's about to overwrite**:

```
Install from https://github.com/someone/entire-foo? The repository is not listed in the plugin index.
```

Nothing there mentions that `ci` is about to be replaced. That's the actual gap — uninformed replacement, not replacement.

## The sharper half you haven't seen yet

There's a variant with **no confirmation at all**. Look at the URL branch:

```go
} else {
    trusted = idxErr == nil && idx.HasRepoURL(repoURL)
}
if !trusted { ...confirm... }
```

If you pass a URL that *is* in the index, `trusted` becomes true, the prompt is skipped, and `expectedName` is still empty. So `entire plugin install <listed-url> --force` can replace a different plugin with **no prompt and no name check** — even though, for a listed URL, the index entry tells us exactly what the plugin should be called.

## What I'd do instead

**For an index-listed URL** — derive `expectedName` from the index entry (needs a small `FindByRepoURL`, since only `HasRepoURL` exists today). The existing guard then applies and the no-prompt path is closed properly, with no new behavior.

**For an unlisted URL** — keep `--force` doing its job, but name the casualty in the prompt that already exists:

```
Install from https://github.com/someone/entire-foo?
The repository is not listed in the plugin index.
This will replace the installed plugin "ci" (currently from https://github.com/entireio/entire-ci).
```

With `--yes`, the same line as a warning.

That preserves every legitimate use — repair, re-pin, moving a plugin to a new repo, replacing a local-dev build — and only adds information where the user was previously making a decision blind. It also leaves doctor's flow untouched, since its URL always matches the manifest.

Want me to do it that way? And I'd still fix the two Mediums as reported — the nil-index one and appending `--allow-unverified` to those three Fix strings, which is the same doctor code path.

Your pushback changed the fix, and for the better. Pushed as `87447c12c`.

## You were right, and checking doctor proved it

All three of doctor's `--force` suggestions use `m.RepoURL` — **the manifest of the plugin being repaired**. So doctor always says "reinstall *this* plugin from where *it* came from," and the repo matches by construction. My proposed guard would never have fired on doctor's advice.

But it *would* have fired on something real: `entire-sem` → `entire-graph` are the same plugin at the same commit in your org right now. Someone moving `graph` to the new repo with `--force` is doing exactly what `--force` is for, and I'd have blocked them. Refusing was the wrong instinct.

The actual defect is narrower than the finding framed it: **uninformed replacement, not replacement**. The confirmation says "Install from `<url>`?" and never mentions which installed plugin is about to be overwritten — and the *remote* picks that name.

## What I did instead

**Index-listed URL** — takes its expected name from the catalog entry via a new `FindByRepoURL`. This closes a sharper variant neither the finding nor my earlier assessment mentioned: a URL that's in the index is `trusted`, so it installs with **no prompt at all** and no name check. That path is now covered by the existing guard, with no behavior change for anyone.

**Unlisted URL** — `--force` keeps working, including repo moves. It just reports what it displaced:

```
Warning: replaced plugin "ci", which was installed from https://github.com/entireio/entire-ci.
```

That's the URL to put things back. A same-repo reinstall stays silent, so repair flows are unchanged.

One honest limitation: this lands *after* the replace, not as a prompt. The remote-declared name isn't known until the metadata clone runs inside the install, and prompting from the library layer would be the wrong shape. Since `--force` is an explicit "overwrite" signal, information-after beats a refusal — but it is weaker than a pre-confirmation, and worth knowing.

## The two Mediums

**Nil index** — confirmed the chain: `idx` nil → `Find` returns nil on a nil receiver → every dependency reported "not in the plugin index" → non-zero exit *after* the install printed success. That contradicted the contract written four lines below the call site. Now skipped with a warning that names the index as unavailable.

**Doctor's unworkable fix** — extracted `reinstallCommand`, which carries `--allow-unverified` when the manifest records it. The separate "installed without checksum verification" issue still suggests `plugin upgrade`, which already inherits the flag and needed no change.

## One process note

`mise run test:ci` failed once mid-way and my grep didn't capture what. Rather than assume it was one of this branch's three known flakes, I ran it twice more — both clean, 59 + 4 tests. Two clean runs after an uncaptured failure isn't proof, but it's the evidence I have and I'd rather say so than call it green without qualification.

All three findings resolved with the reasoning recorded, including that the first fix isn't what was suggested and why.

content.text:
You're right about the diagnosis. Three facts:

**Nothing in production uses it.** The only non-test mention of `file://` in the codebase is a comment. Nine test files depend on it.

**A `file://` plugin repo can't even complete an install.** `releaseAssetBaseURL` requires an http(s) repo URL, so a `file://` repo fails at asset download unless the plugin declares a `download_url`. So as a *plugin source* it's near-useless in production, which supports your read that it's there for tests.

**But `git daemon` would make the boundary worse, not better.** `git daemon` serves `git://` — the scheme I removed from the allowlist an hour ago as unauthenticated and unencrypted. Using it in tests means putting `git://` back, trading a local-filesystem scheme for a MITM-able *network* one. The other options are no better: smart-HTTP needs `git-http-backend` via CGI *and* `http://` back in the allowlist; `ssh://` needs an sshd. Every test transport needs *some* scheme, and `file://` is the least dangerous of the three.

So the instinct is right but the proposed remedy inverts it.

## What would actually achieve your goal

Gate `file://` on a test sentinel, so production's allowlist is `{https, ssh, scp-like}` and tests still work. The repo already does this everywhere — `ENTIRE_TEST_GIT_HERMETIC`, `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY`, `ENTIRE_TEST_AUTH_STORE_FILE` — with `testing.Testing()` for in-process and an env var for the spawned-binary tests, which CLAUDE.md explicitly documents as the pattern.

It's not a real weakening either: anyone who can set your env vars already has code execution.

## What it's actually worth, honestly

The attacker-reachable path is a hostile **index entry** with a `file://` `repo_url`. What that buys today: `git ls-remote` probes the local filesystem and the error may reveal whether a path is a git repo. Then the install dies at asset download. So — minor information disclosure, no execution, no install.

Against that, the cost is a second validation *policy*. And there's one production use that genuinely works: `--index file:///srv/plugin-index` for an air-gapped or internal catalog. The index only needs `index.json`, so unlike a plugin repo it functions end-to-end — and after the settings removal, the index URL is user-supplied only, never attacker-chosen.

That suggests the sharpest split follows the trust boundary rather than the scheme: **`file://` stays for the index (user-supplied, works, plausible), and goes for plugin repo URLs (catalog-supplied, can't install anyway) except under the test sentinel.**

My hesitation is that this means two named policies over one core — and two validators drifting is precisely what bit this branch twice, first on `http://`/absolute paths and then on the scp-like form. I'd structure it as two thin wrappers over one function with an explicit parameter, never two implementations, but the risk is real and worth naming before I do it.

## My recommendation

Do it, with the split above. The information disclosure is small, but the principle is right and the cost is bounded — and "a `file://` plugin repo can't complete an install anyway" means removing it from that path costs nothing real.

If you'd rather not add the second policy, the honest fallback is to leave the allowlist alone and document *why* `file://` is there — but I'd not pretend that's as good.

Done — `ea46af2c3`. Lint 0 issues, and I ran the full suite four more times, all clean.

To answer your check first: **yes, test-only everywhere** — and that stricter reading is what landed. My original proposal kept `file://` for the index URL in production. I dropped it, because it needed two validation policies over one core, and two policies drifting is the exact failure this branch already hit twice (first `http://`/absolute paths, then the scp-like form). Your version is simpler and removes that risk.

## What shipped

Production allowlist is now `{https://, ssh://, user@host:path}`. `file://` is accepted only under `testing.Testing()`, plus `ENTIRE_TEST_ALLOW_FILE_REMOTES` for the integration harness — which spawns the real binary, where `testing.Testing()` is false. That's the same shape the harness already uses for config, cache, and token isolation.

The gate is a `var` rather than a `func` so the *shipped* rejection path is reachable from a test (`testing.Testing()` is otherwise always true where the test runs). Same seam as `postPluginVersionCheck` in that package.

Worth restating the thing that made the git-daemon route a non-starter: `git daemon` serves `git://` — the scheme I'd removed an hour earlier as unauthenticated. It would have traded a local-filesystem transport for a MITM-able network one. Your instinct about the boundary was right; that particular remedy would have inverted it.

## The intermittent CI failures — now explained

I've had two `test:ci` failures I couldn't capture, and I've been saying "probably the known flakes" without evidence. So I looped until it reproduced — it didn't, four clean runs — and then checked the toolchain instead:

```
go.mod / mise.toml:  go 1.26.4
```

My notes record a darwin `-race` subprocess-segfault as a **Go bug fixed in 1.26.5**. The pin is one patch behind it. That fits both failures: intermittent, in spawned-subprocess integration tests, unreproducible on retry.

Bumping the pin is the actual fix, but it's a repo-wide toolchain change touching CI and every developer, so it's well outside this PR. Worth raising separately — it's making "is CI green?" a noisier signal than it should be for whoever reviews this.

## Where things stand

No open trail findings. All review threads resolved. No new PR comments. The branch is ~30 commits from this session on top of the original 8, all green.

Still open and unchanged: the `platforms` field (warns but never enforces, and lives in the catalog rather than with the author), `auto_installed` orphan tracking, the two notions of "official", `entire upgrade` naming, the `main.go` redaction follow-up, and adding `graph` to the published index.

content.text:
Confirmed, and it's sharper than I'd been repeating. Two lines in `mise.toml` already ship an Entire-owned binary — including an `entire-agent-*` one — through mise's `go:` backend:

```toml
"go:github.com/entireio/roger-roger/cmd/entire-agent-roger-roger" = 'latest'
```

And `versioncheck.go` already has `installManagerBrew` / `Mise` / `Scoop`, detects which one installed the CLI, and emits the right upgrade command. So the "delegate to a package manager" idea isn't foreign here — it's already how the CLI distributes *itself* and at least one plugin-shaped binary.

## On brew specifically: I'd say no, but for a boring reason

**Windows.** This CLI supports it — there's a `test-windows` CI job, `.exe` naming, and a symlink→hardlink→copy fallback for machines without Developer Mode. Homebrew has no Windows story, so brew-under-the-hood abandons those users or forces a second mechanism, at which point you haven't deleted the machinery, you've added a branch to it.

Second problem: **who writes the formula.** Today a plugin author publishes a GitHub release and adds one JSON entry. With brew they'd need a Ruby DSL formula and either a slot in your tap (you become a bottleneck) or their own tap (which the user must `brew tap` first). That's a meaningful tax on "anyone can write a plugin."

And you'd lose `install <git-url>` — the one genuinely new capability in this PR, and the thing no package manager gives you.

## The stronger version of your question is mise, not brew

`mise use ubi:entireio/entire-ci` fetches a GitHub release binary for your platform and puts it on PATH — which is **exactly** what this PR's asset-download machinery does, generically, cross-platform, with zero per-plugin packaging. No formula, no tap, no index entry.

That would delete a great deal: asset-name conventions and the `darwin_all` handling, checksum fetching and verification, the git-synced index with its TTL, flock, and stale-on-offline logic, and — via `mise` dependencies — most of `requires[]`. Roughly the majority of the 5,500 lines here.

## What I actually think

The honest position is that **the ecosystem doesn't yet justify owning distribution**. One shipped plugin (`ci`), plus `upgrade` and the `graph`/`brain` pair. This PR builds a package manager for that, and it's found something real in every one of the seven review rounds — which is what owning distribution costs you, permanently.

The floor isn't nothing, though: `entire plugin install <git-url>` for the URL case, plus a documented `mise use ubi:…` line for the curated ones. That keeps the capability nobody else provides and drops the parts three tools already do better.

Two caveats I'd hold honestly. Delegating means requiring mise, which a non-developer on Windows won't have — and that's the same population brew fails, so it doesn't disappear by switching tools. And I haven't verified what `ubi` does about checksum verification; if it doesn't verify, the strongest argument in this PR (refuse unauthenticated downloads by default) would be a genuine regression, and I'd want that checked before anyone acts on this.

## What I'd do with it

Not touch this branch. It's green, reviewed, and the security work stands on its own regardless of who ends up doing the fetching.

But this is the second independent line of reasoning arriving at "should this exist at this scope" — the architecture review got there from line count and demand, you've got there from spec ownership. That's worth putting to Thomas as a real question rather than a footnote, and it's a better question *now* than after third-party plugins adopt `entire-plugin.yml` and the schema becomes load-bearing.

If you want, I can spend a few minutes checking whether `ubi` verifies checksums and whether `mise use ubi:entireio/entire-ci` works today — concrete evidence would make that conversation much shorter.

content.text:
Both done in `bd570cd59`. Full CI green, lint 0 issues.

## Lstat

Two sites in `plugin_index.go`, both asking whether *our own* files exist — the `.git` marking a directory as a clone, and the sync marker whose mtime drives the TTL. `Stat` follows symlinks, so a `.git` symlink pointing elsewhere would answer "yes, this is a clone" for a directory that isn't one. Matches the convention `062d8bb3a` set.

I left one `Stat` alone: `plugin_group.go` checking a **user-supplied** path for the "did you mean `./name`" hint. That's not a file we own, and following a symlink to a real file is the helpful behavior there.

## Bounded reads — and the bigger one you pointed at indirectly

Both `os.ReadFile` calls are now capped: `index.json` at 8 MiB (cloned from a remote catalog) and `manifest.yml` at 1 MiB (ours, but in a user-writable directory). They error rather than truncate, since a truncated file parses as valid-but-wrong.

But chasing "for the metadata it can be quite small" led somewhere more interesting: **`entire-plugin.yml` never goes through `ReadFile`**. It arrives via `git show <tag>:entire-plugin.yml` through `cmd.Output()` — which buffers stdout with **no ceiling at all**. Same for `ls-remote`. Both read remote-controlled data: whatever refs a repository advertises, and whatever an author committed. A hostile repo listed in a catalog could have handed back an arbitrarily large response.

So `runGitQuiet` now takes an explicit cap per call — **64 KiB** for metadata (a name, a description, a short requires list), 16 MiB for refs, 4 KiB for `--quiet` commands that should print nothing. Your instinct about metadata being small was right; it just wasn't the code path it looked like.

One consequence worth flagging: capping stdout meant reading through a pipe instead of `cmd.Output()`, which empties `ExitError.Stderr`. So stderr is captured directly and folded into the error, and `stderrSuffix` is gone — it existed only to dig detail out of `ExitError`, and the reuse review had already flagged it as the sixth copy of that pattern in the repo. The riskiest part was the benign "no metadata file" branch, which matched on `stderrSuffix(err)`; it now matches the error text, which carries the same stderr. `TestFetchPluginMetadataAtTag_NoFileIsNilNil` covers it and passes.

Also deliberate: `readFileLimited` returns `os.Open`'s error **unwrapped**, because `LoadPluginManifest` tests it with `errors.Is` against `os.ErrNotExist` to report an absent manifest as `(nil, nil)`. Wrapping it would have silently turned "no manifest" into a hard error — I added a `//nolint:wrapcheck` with that reason rather than let someone tidy it later.

New tests cover an oversize `entire-plugin.yml` end-to-end through the real git path, a normal-sized one still parsing, and `readFileLimited` at/over the limit plus the missing-file case.

content.text:
Short answer: **it's already guaranteed**, in three independent places — but nothing checked it, and writing the check found a bug sitting right next to it.

## What already holds, and how

The archive entry's name only *selects* what to extract. The destination is `pluginBinaryName(name)` → always `entire-<name>[.exe]`, and `name` has already been through `validatePluginName` (no separators, no `.`/`..`, no leading `-`, no reserved `agent-`). So the written filename is ours by construction, not by validation.

Exactly one binary, also structural: all three extraction branches `return` on the first match, so the loops can't write twice. A *differently* named `entire-*` entry in the same archive is ignored — that's the "plugin claims a second command name" case.

And local installs are gated the same way: `plugin_store.go` refuses a source basename without the prefix.

The gap was that all of this is emergent. A refactor that used the archive's own entry name, or kept looping past a match, would have silently let a plugin put a second command on `PATH` — possibly someone else's.

## The bug the test found

My fixture built a tar from a Go map, so entry order was randomized — and `bin/entire-mine` won over the root `entire-mine`. Selection was "first basename match **in archive order**".

That's a real non-determinism: matching is by basename, and archives legitimately hold several candidates — the binary at the root, the same name nested under a versioned directory (goreleaser's `wrap_in_directory`), and things like `completions/entire-<name>`. Which one you installed depended on the order the author's tar happened to be built in. The `/simplify` review had flagged this as a "first match wins" smell; it took a test to show it actually bites.

`preferredArchiveEntry` now picks **shallowest path, then lexicographic** — encoding the convention that the real binary is at the root or one level down, and a same-named file deeper in the tree is a completion script. For tar that costs a second pass, since the stream can't seek backwards.

## On "or more?"

Today it's strictly one, and I'd leave it there unless there's demand. Allowing several means one install can claim several *command names* — which reopens exactly the squatting problem the `ExpectedName` work just closed for the single-binary case. If it's ever wanted, each extra name would need the same reconciliation against something the user or catalog asserted, not just the remote's say-so.

One process note: my block edit accidentally deleted `fileSHA256`, which sat between the two extraction functions. The compiler caught it immediately, but it's a reminder that these bulk replacements need the build as a backstop — which is why I run it after every edit rather than at the end.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

68		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, pluginGitTimeout)

65	#### Repository URLs are a security boundary
66	
67	Every repo URL is validated by `validatePluginRepoURL` before it reaches the git CLI, and every git invocation passes `--` before its positionals. Both layers exist because repo URLs are attacker-influenced: they arrive from `index.json` entries and from `--index`/`ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`.
68	
69	git parses an option-shaped positional as an option, and `--upload-pack=<cmd>` is shell-interpreted — with no positional repository left, it runs against the *ambient* repo's `origin`. So a catalog entry like `--upload-pack=curl … | sh; git-upload-pack` would execute arbitrary commands during an index-resolved install, which by design never prompts. Dependency planning is the tightest path: it contacts a dependency's repository — now always an index-listed one — *before* the install confirmation.
70	
71	Accepted forms are `https://`, `ssh://`, and git's `user@host:path` scp-like syntax. Anything else — a leading `-`, a bare name, a relative or absolute path, `file://`, git's command-executing `ext::` transport — is rejected.
72	
73	`file://` is accepted **only under test**. Nothing in production needs it: a `file://` plugin repository cannot complete an install, because `releaseAssetBaseURL` requires an http(s) repo URL to locate the asset, and `install ./path` is the supported way to use a local build. Its only real consumer was the test suite, and a security allowlist should not be widened to pay for test convenience — the alternative transports a test could use are worse, since `git daemon` serves `git://`, exactly the scheme rejected above. The gate is `testing.Testing()` plus `ENTIRE_TEST_ALLOW_FILE_REMOTES` for the integration harness, which spawns the real binary where `testing.Testing()` is false. Being able to set that variable already implies code execution, so it is not a weakening; what it buys is that a hostile catalog entry cannot name a local path and use the CLI to probe the filesystem.
74	
75	`http://` and `git://` are deliberately absent. Both are unauthenticated and unencrypted, and the catalog fetched over them decides which repositories install *without a confirmation prompt*, so an attacker who can rewrite the transport chooses the binary — strictly worse than the plaintext-asset case below. Bare absolute paths are rejected because `file://` expresses the same thing unambiguously; narrowing a security boundary beats the convenience.
76

Invalid index entries are dropped like invalid names, so one bad row cannot take out the catalog.

content.text:
Pushed. Second `/simplify` pass done — 14 findings applied, all four agents' scopes covered.

## What the agents found that mattered

Three of these were holes in the *previous* pass's own work, which is the useful kind of finding:

**The cap only ever covered stdout.** `cmd.Stderr` was a plain `bytes.Buffer`. `cmd.Output()` had been supplying a 32 KiB ceiling for free (`prefixSuffixSaver`), and replacing it dropped that — on the stream carrying the remote's sideband, i.e. remote-controlled data by exactly the standard the commit had applied to stdout. `limitedWriter` now caps both, with a different overflow policy per stream: stdout fails, stderr absorbs and drops. Feeding it to `cmd.Stdout` rather than reading a pipe also removed a two-minute wedge — `os/exec` closes the pipe the moment a write fails, where returning early from a pipe read left `Wait()` blocked on a full one until `pluginGitTimeout`.

**Bounding the read still allowed gigabytes of heap.** `tarEntryNames` collected every entry name before filtering. The efficiency agent measured it: entry headers compress to ~4.9 bytes each, so the 512 MiB asset cap admits ~110M entries → ~4.2 GiB of `[]string` — to choose between the one or two entries a real release holds. Worse, a change I'd made earlier in this same session (`make([]string, 0, len(names))` for a `slices.MinFunc` rewrite) added another ~1.7 GiB. A running minimum does the job in one string.

That last one is a direct conflict between two agents: the simplification agent wanted `slices.MinFunc` over a materialized candidate slice, which is cleaner to read but requires the allocation. I took efficiency's side — the memory argument is about attacker-controlled input, the readability one is about taste.

**The `file://` seam test proved nothing.** It swapped `allowLocalGitURL` for its own reimplementation and asserted against that. The policy is now a pure function of both inputs, and the test exercises `underTest=false` — the spawned-binary case an in-process test can't otherwise reach.

## Two user-facing repairs

A dependency install that replaced a plugin from a different repo said nothing, though the top-level install names it — and dependencies are the path confirmed once as a batch, with URLs from the catalog, so an upgrade could repoint a user's fork silently. And doctor's repair command dropped `--pin`, so fixing an unrelated breakage would quietly unpin a plugin held at a version on purpose.

## Skipped, with reasons

- **Stat-sizing `readWithinLimit`** — measured 2.45x faster at 8 MiB, but it lives in `api_cmd.go`, outside this diff, and the real beneficiary is `entire api`. At plugin sizes it's ~9 µs. Cross-scope churn for noise.
- **Inlining `stderrDetail`** (one caller) — it's a named home for the credential-redaction requirement; that's worth 10 lines.
- **Dropping the `idxErr == nil` conjunct** at `plugin_group.go:239` — redundant today because `FindByRepoURL` is nil-safe, but it gates `trusted`, which means "install without a prompt." I'd rather that read as "we loaded a catalog successfully" than depend on a nil-check two files away.

Lint 0 issues, full `test:ci` green including the Vogon canary. Branch is at `f727a8a31`; the only red on the PR remains the human-approval gate.
